promptText: What is the fundamental capability an RNN adds beyond what a plain feedforward network can do for processing sequences?
options: It maintains a fixed-size hidden state that carries a compressed summary of everything seen so far, updated at every step with a reused set of weights
It always processes the entire sequence in parallel using self-attention over every pair of positions
It uses a separate, specially-trained set of weights for each position in the sequence
It converts variable-length input into a fixed one-hot vector before any processing begins
explanation: The RNN's hidden state is the network's only channel of memory, updated by the same learned weights at every timestep, which is exactly the capability a feedforward network's fixed-size, order-blind input lacks.

promptText: An RNN reuses the same weight matrices W_hh and W_xh at every timestep (parameter sharing across time). What is the direct payoff of this design choice?
options: The parameter count stays fixed regardless of sequence length, and the model learns one transition rule that generalizes to sequences longer or shorter than any seen in training
It guarantees the model will never suffer from vanishing or exploding gradients
It allows the hidden-state dimensionality to grow automatically as the sequence gets longer
It removes the need for a nonlinear activation function in the recurrence
explanation: Because the same three weight structures are reused at every step, total parameter count is fixed by hidden and input dimensionality alone, letting one trained transition rule apply uniformly to sequences of any length.

promptText: Why do vanilla RNNs traditionally use tanh rather than ReLU as the hidden-state activation function?
options: tanh bounds the hidden state's values within a fixed range, preventing unbounded growth from compounding since the same value is fed back into the recurrence at every subsequent step
tanh has a strictly larger derivative than ReLU everywhere, which speeds up convergence
ReLU cannot mathematically be combined with a matrix multiplication
tanh guarantees gradients never vanish across long sequences
explanation: Because the hidden state recycles into the same computation at every step, an unbounded activation like ReLU would let any tendency toward amplification compound across timesteps into runaway growth; tanh's bounded range avoids that specific risk.

promptText: Why is 'unrolling' the recurrent cell into a chain of copies necessary in order to train an RNN with backpropagation?
options: Standard backpropagation requires an explicit, acyclic computation graph, and the self-referential loop (h_t depends on h_{t-1}) must be expanded into a finite chain before the chain rule can be applied
Unrolling is only a hardware requirement for GPUs and is unnecessary when training on a CPU
Unrolling converts the sequential computation into fully parallel computation with no remaining dependency between steps
Unrolling is used only during inference, never during training
explanation: A self-referential loop isn't directly differentiable; unrolling expands it into an equivalent finite chain of operations so ordinary backpropagation (BPTT) can apply the chain rule step by step backward through it.

promptText: Why is gradient clipping applied essentially by default when training any vanilla RNN?
options: Exploding gradients are a structural risk of the architecture, caused by repeated multiplication by the same recurrent weight matrix across timesteps, so a single unusually large gradient can otherwise destabilize the model in one update
Gradient clipping eliminates the vanishing gradient problem as a side effect
Gradient clipping reduces the total number of parameters that need to be trained
Gradient clipping allows the hidden state to be computed in parallel across timesteps
explanation: Because the same W_hh is multiplied in repeatedly during BPTT, an eigenvalue above 1 can cause gradients to blow up; clipping caps the damage a single bad batch can do, at negligible cost, which is why it is applied as cheap default insurance.

promptText: Why is the initial hidden state h0 typically set to a vector of zeros rather than random values?
options: Zero represents a neutral 'no context yet' starting point that is consistent across every sequence, so differences in output can be attributed entirely to actual input content rather than an arbitrary random start
Random initialization of h0 would make tanh's output become unbounded
Zero initialization is required to prevent the weight matrices W_hh and W_xh from ever being updated
Zero initialization guarantees the network will not experience exploding gradients later in training
explanation: A consistent, known starting state avoids introducing extra variance the network would otherwise have to learn to be robust to, and keeps runs comparable across sequences and reproducible across seeds.

promptText: In BPTT, the local gradient propagated backward one step is roughly tanh'(z) multiplied by W_hh's transpose. Why does this make the vanishing gradient problem worse than the weight matrix's eigenvalues alone would predict?
options: tanh'(z) is guaranteed to be at most 1 and shrinks well below 1 whenever a unit is even moderately saturated, so this factor compounds with W_hh's eigenvalue structure at every single step, on top of whatever the matrix alone would cause
tanh'(z) grows without bound as z increases, which offsets any shrinkage caused by W_hh's eigenvalues
tanh'(z) is applied only once, at the very last timestep, so it cannot affect gradients reaching early timesteps
tanh'(z) is irrelevant to BPTT, which multiplies only by W_hh and never by activation derivatives
explanation: Since tanh'(z) = 1 - tanh(z)^2 is at most 1 and often much smaller near saturation, it multiplies in alongside W_hh's eigenvalue at every backward step, meaning even a perfectly orthogonal W_hh does not by itself guarantee stable gradient flow.

promptText: Why is global norm-based gradient clipping generally preferred over element-wise (value-based) clipping specifically for recurrent architectures?
options: Norm-based clipping rescales the entire gradient vector by one shared factor, exactly preserving its direction, whereas element-wise clipping distorts direction by clamping some coordinates and not others — and an RNN's gradient is an accumulated sum of many correlated per-timestep contributions where preserving that balance matters
Norm-based clipping is computationally cheaper because it avoids a square-root computation entirely
Element-wise clipping cannot be implemented for matrices, only for individual scalars
Norm-based clipping removes the need for any learning-rate schedule during training
explanation: Rescaling the whole gradient vector by one factor is mathematically equivalent to taking a smaller step in the same direction, while clamping coordinates independently rotates the vector away from the true accumulated gradient direction.

promptText: Why does truncated BPTT introduce a bias into the gradient estimate rather than simply adding random noise around the true gradient?
options: It systematically and identically discards, on every single training step, any gradient contribution from dependencies beyond the truncation window, so it consistently underweights or zeroes out long-range signal rather than varying randomly around the true value
It randomly samples a different truncation window on each training step, which averages out to the true gradient over many steps
It only affects the forward pass computation and has no bearing on how gradients are computed
It effectively doubles the learning rate applied to the truncated portion of each sequence
explanation: The discarding of long-range gradient paths happens the same way every time, making it a consistent, structural underestimate rather than noise that would average out — which is why it becomes a real ceiling on learnable dependency length, not just added variance.

promptText: A colleague proposes fixing an RNN's vanishing gradient problem by simply increasing the hidden-state dimensionality. Why won't this work?
options: Hidden-state size controls how much information the network can store at a single timestep (capacity), but does nothing to change the eigenvalue structure of W_hh or the repeated multiplicative gradient dynamics that actually cause vanishing gradients
A larger hidden state automatically pushes W_hh's largest eigenvalue above 1, converting the vanishing problem into an exploding one
Hidden-state dimensionality is fixed by the vocabulary size and cannot be changed independently
Larger hidden states raise the lower bound of tanh's derivative, structurally eliminating the vanishing problem
explanation: Capacity (how much can be stored) and gradient flow (whether training signal can reach early weights) are separate problems; a bigger matrix can have exactly the same problematic eigenvalue spectrum as a smaller one, which is why the actual fix (LSTMs) redesigns the update mechanism instead.

promptText: Why does a bidirectional RNN require entirely separate weight sets for its forward and backward passes rather than sharing one set?
options: The forward pass learns a transition rule for predicting from past context while the backward pass learns a different rule for predicting from future context read in reverse — these are genuinely different functions, and forcing shared weights would create conflicting gradient pressure toward two different optimal transitions
Sharing weights between the two passes would make the architecture mathematically identical to a unidirectional RNN
Separate weights exist only to allow the two passes to run on separate GPUs, with no effect on what is learned
Shared weights would violate the constant-memory-per-stream property that makes RNNs useful on edge devices
explanation: 'What tends to follow X' and 'what tends to precede X' are different statistical regularities even over identical data, so a single shared weight set would be pulled toward a compromised average of two different optimal transition functions.

promptText: Why does an RNN's memory footprint stay constant at inference regardless of sequence length, while its memory footprint during training grows with sequence length?
options: At inference only the current hidden state must be kept in memory (previous states can be discarded), but BPTT's backward pass needs the cached activations from every timestep, since it computes local gradients through each of them while walking backward
Training always uses a larger hidden-state dimensionality than inference by architectural design
Inference always uses truncated BPTT internally, while training never does
Training requires bidirectional processing while inference uses only a unidirectional pass
explanation: The backward pass processes timesteps in reverse order and needs each step's cached input, previous hidden state, and pre-activation value to compute that step's local Jacobian, so nothing can be discarded until the backward pass has used it.

promptText: A trained RNN's recurrent weight matrix has a largest eigenvalue magnitude of 1.05, and sequences run 200 steps long. What is the most accurate assessment, and why is this 'just above 1' case particularly hard to catch compared to an obviously large eigenvalue like 3.0?
options: 1.05 raised to the 200th power is roughly a 17,000x amplification, so exploding gradients are very likely; and because small weight perturbations during training can push the eigenvalue back and forth across 1, instability near the boundary tends to build slowly and look like healthy training for many steps before suddenly compounding — unlike an eigenvalue of 3.0, which diverges quickly and obviously
1.05 is close enough to 1 that no meaningful amplification occurs even after 200 steps, so training proceeds normally
An eigenvalue of 1.05 always causes vanishing gradients, since any value under 2 is considered small in this context
Eigenvalue magnitude only governs the forward pass, not gradient propagation, so this has no bearing on training stability
explanation: 1.05^200 is approximately 17,292; unlike a dramatically large eigenvalue that diverges obviously and immediately, a value just above 1 can drift across the stability boundary unpredictably during training, producing a slow-building instability that is much harder to catch through casual monitoring.

promptText: Orthogonal initialization sets W_hh so that all its singular values equal 1 at the start of training. Why does this matter specifically for gradient flow during BPTT, rather than only for forward-pass activation stability?
options: The backward pass repeatedly multiplies the propagated gradient by a Jacobian involving W_hh's transpose, which has the same singular values as W_hh itself, so starting all singular values at exactly 1 means the earliest backward multiplications neither shrink nor grow the gradient's norm, giving training a stable starting point before any drift begins
Orthogonal matrices have no transpose, so the backward-pass computation involving W_hh is skipped entirely
Orthogonal initialization guarantees that tanh will never saturate at any timestep throughout training
Orthogonal initialization only affects W_xh, which governs the forward pass exclusively and has no role in gradient computation
explanation: A matrix's transpose shares its singular values with the original, so an orthogonally-initialized W_hh (all singular values 1) keeps the backward-pass Jacobian's norm-preserving property at initialization — a fact about backward-pass gradient magnitude specifically, distinct from forward-pass activation stability.

promptText: State-space models like Mamba are described as combining RNN-style constant-memory inference with Transformer-style parallel training. What specific structural choice enables this combination?
options: The recurrence is structured to be linear (or linear-in-the-state), so the whole-sequence computation can be reformulated as a convolution or parallel-scan operation for parallel training, while the identical underlying recurrence still supports a sequential, constant-memory step-by-step update at inference
The model trains two entirely separate networks — an RNN for inference and a Transformer for training — and distills one into the other afterward
It replaces the recurrence with full quadratic self-attention during training and switches to a static lookup table for inference
It removes the hidden state entirely and relies solely on positional encodings to represent history
explanation: Because the recurrence's mathematical form (linear/structured) admits an equivalent convolutional or parallel-scan formulation, the exact same computation can be executed in parallel across all positions during training and step-by-step with constant memory during inference — the same underlying math viewed two ways.
